Mapping this to a downcast would answer the top of a chain with no rest: right today, and silently wrong the day upstream wraps something.
calls.strconv.ParseUint: The two parsers disagree about input the SOURCE REJECTS. The target accepts a leading `+`, so `+5` parses there and fails here; and the source takes a base and a bit size, of which only base 10 at 64 bits is the target's `parse` at all. A version parser is exactly where that matters -- the difference is invisible on valid input and changes which strings are accepted.
calls.strings.EqualFold: The source compares under Unicode SIMPLE CASE FOLDING. The target's `eq_ignore_ascii_case` folds only ASCII, and comparing `to_lowercase()` is case MAPPING rather than folding; they differ on the Kelvin sign, on final sigma, and on the Turkish dotless i. Each of those compares equal in the source and unequal in at least one target spelling, on input no test would think to write.

unmappable_calls.reason: Calls into libraries that do not come along and CANNOT be mapped, each with the reason it cannot. Distinct from a call the pack has simply not reached: that one refuses saying a mapping is owed, and this one refuses saying a mapping would be WRONG. Every entry is a case where the target has something that looks like the source's call and differs on input a test would not think to write -- a parser that accepts one more string, a comparison that folds a different alphabet, a chain-walker with no chain. Emitting the near-equivalent is precisely the failure this engine exists to prevent, and the near-equivalents are the tempting ones, so the reason is written where the next reader will look for it.

types.sync.Mutex: The two guard different things. The source's mutex guards a CRITICAL SECTION and sits beside the fields it protects -- `mu sync.Mutex` next to `pool [256]byte`, locked and unlocked around the code that touches them -- and nothing in the type system ties the two together. The target's mutex OWNS what it protects: `Mutex<[u8; 256]>`, and the only way to reach the bytes is to hold the lock. Mapping the type alone would emit a lock guarding nothing beside fields anyone can reach, which compiles and protects nothing. What it wants is the struct RESHAPED so the mutex wraps the fields it stands next to -- a decision about which fields those are, which the source does not record and the engine cannot infer from adjacency.
types.fmt.State: An interface the source's formatting machinery passes to a custom formatter, carrying the flags and width from the verb. The target's formatter is a different design -- its own trait, its own options object -- and nothing in it corresponds field for field. A type mapping would name a trait the target does not have.
types.math/rand.Source64: A random source. The target's standard library has no random number generation at all, so this is a dependency decision about the ported crate rather than a spelling -- the same answer the digest constructors get, for the same reason.
types.time.Time: The source's instant is a wall clock reading with a monotonic reading attached and a location beside it. The target's standard library splits those: `SystemTime` is the wall clock and has no monotonic part, `Instant` is monotonic and cannot be formatted or compared across processes, and neither carries a zone. Any single mapping silently drops one of the three, and which one is a decision about what the ported program uses the value FOR.

unmappable_types.reason: Types from libraries that do not come along and CANNOT be mapped, each with the reason it cannot. The mirror of the unmappable CALLS table, and it exists for the same distinction: a type the pack has not reached refuses saying a mapping is owed, and one it has looked at refuses saying a mapping would be wrong. Every entry here is a case where the target has a type of the same NAME or the same rough purpose and a different shape -- a mutex that owns its data rather than sitting beside it, a clock split in three. Emitting the near-equivalent gives a program that compiles and guards nothing, or one that quietly loses a reading. Naming them is worth more than leaving each to be rediscovered.

facts.unsafe_layout_only: A type whose EVERY reference in its own package sits inside the source's `unsafe.Pointer` escape hatch. That hatch is the source's way out of its own type system, and a type reached only through it is not describing a value -- it is describing how the SOURCE RUNTIME lays one out in memory. The target does not share that layout, so there is nothing for the fields to mean. `xxhash`'s `sliceHeader` is the case the rule was measured on: two fields mirroring a slice's representation so a string can be reinterpreted as a byte slice without copying. Ported naively it arrives as an ordinary struct in a crate that denies `unsafe`, whose fields could never do what they were for, and which a reader has no way to identify as residue -- a blind reviewer of this engine's output named it the single most decisive evidence that the code was mechanically translated, and observed from the other side that no Rust author would invent it because `as_bytes()` already does the job for free. EVERY reference must be inside the hatch: a type used both ways is a real type that also happens to be reinterpreted somewhere, and refusing it would be refusing the author's work on the strength of one use. This refuses by NAME rather than dropping the type for being unreferenced -- see the R2f entry in build/REORG-DRAIN.md for why reachability was the wrong instrument.

binary_string.reason: What a source STRING becomes when its content is not text. The source's string is a byte string -- it holds arbitrary bytes and is the idiomatic bag of them -- and the target's is guaranteed UTF-8, so the usual mapping is right only for the ones that are text. `magic = "xxh\x06"` is a four-byte framing prefix, never displayed and never compared as text, and a reviewer named it typed as `&str` among their most decisive evidence. The trap they described is concrete rather than stylistic: the trailing byte is a format-version tag, and the target's string literals admit `\xNN` only up to `\x7F`. Bump that tag past it and the literal stops compiling; the natural repair spells one character as TWO bytes, silently turning a length of 4 into 5 and shifting every offset in the marshaled layout. A byte array makes that a type error instead of a wire-format break. RECOGNISED, not guessed: a string constant whose bytes are not all printable text is binary. A byte the source had to write as an escape because it cannot be typed is exactly the evidence, and the common text escapes -- newline, tab, carriage return -- are text and stay text. BY VALUE, not by reference. A constant is materialised at every use anyway, so a reference to a static array buys an indirection and nothing else -- and a reviewer reading the referenced form called it an awkward hybrid that reads like an accident. The literal dereferences because a byte-string literal IS a reference in the target, and the constant wants what it points at.

bit_pattern_constants.reason: Which integer constants the target spells in hexadecimal. A count and a bit pattern wear the same syntax and are read differently: a count is a quantity and belongs in decimal, while a mask, seed, or multiplier is read as its bits and belongs in hex, where a reviewer can check it against the specification that defines it. A reviewer of this engine's output said exactly that, having had to run a script to verify five hash primes written in decimal. The TYPE decides and magnitude cannot: measured over the corpus, seven package constants exceed 32 bits and two of them -- the ticks between 1582 and the Unix epoch -- are counts typed at the source's counting integer, while the five that are patterns are typed at a fixed-width unsigned one, which is what an author reaches for when the bits are the point. `min_value` keeps small flags and enumerations readable as numbers, since a one-byte value spelled `0x07` gains nothing over `7`.

readable_literals.reason:
How a long DECIMAL literal is spelled so a reader can see its magnitude. The target groups digits with an underscore and the source does not, so a value carried over unchanged is correct and unreadable: two reviewers independently picked out `10000000` and `1000000` on nearby lines as indistinguishable at a glance, and they differ by a factor of ten. Grouping is from the RIGHT, which is what makes the groups mean thousands.

Applies only where the literal stays decimal. A value the type says is a bit pattern is spelled in hexadecimal by `bit_pattern_constants` and grouped by its own convention, and running both would produce a hex literal with decimal grouping.

`min_digits` is 5 rather than 4, because a four-digit number is read at a glance and a year is the common one -- `2026_` reads worse than `2026`.

allocation.empty_with_capacity_reason: `make([]T, 0, n)` -- a sequence with NO elements and room for n. The target's growable sequence spells exactly that, and the two agree on everything a program can observe: length zero, capacity n, no allocation beyond it until the n+1st push. The ZERO length is required, not incidental. `make([]T, n)` gives n ZERO ELEMENTS and `Vec::with_capacity(n)` gives none -- the same number in two different roles, which is exactly the shape of mistake that compiles and means something else. Every other shape refuses by name.
allocation.filled_reason: `make([]T, n)` -- a sequence of n ZERO elements. `{0}` is the count and `{1}` is the element type's zero value, which the pack already answers for elsewhere and which is what the source fills with. Exact where the zero is one the pack knows, and refused where it is not: a sequence filled with a value the engine guessed is a program that starts from somewhere the source did not.
allocation.owned_from_slice_reason: How a BORROW of a sequence becomes the owned sequence a result asks for. The source's slice of an array is a value it hands back -- `id[:]` on a value receiver slices the receiver's own copy -- and the target's `&self.0[..]` borrows what the receiver owns, which does not fit a result declared as the owned form. Naming the conversion here rather than in code keeps it a target spelling: a target that called it something else would change this entry and nothing else.
allocation.reason: How the source's allocating builtin becomes the target's. Its own table rather than a row in the function map because its first argument is a TYPE and its meaning changes with its arity -- two things a form keyed by callee identity cannot express. Only the sequence shapes are here. `make(map[K]V)` and `make(chan T)` are absent and refuse by name: a map's target form is a decision about which map, and a channel is a concurrency primitive whose target counterpart is a decision about the ported program rather than a spelling.

sequence_append.reason: How the source's `append` becomes the target's. The two do NOT correspond as expressions: the source's returns a new sequence and may or may not share the old one's storage, and the target's mutates in place and returns nothing. So the translation is of the whole STATEMENT, not of the call inside it. `b = append(b, ...)` -- the same name on both sides -- is the shape that carries across, because there the source's 'may share storage' question has one answer: the result replaces the original and nothing else observes the difference. `c = append(b, ...)` refuses by name: the source leaves whether `c` and `b` share storage to the capacity at run time, and both target answers -- extend `b` and alias it, or clone -- are a different program on one of the two paths. SPREAD or not decides which form: `append(b, xs...)` adds the elements OF xs and `append(b, x)` adds x itself. Nothing in the tree distinguished them until the front end recorded it, so the two would have translated the same way and one of them wrongly. Several plain elements at once refuse: the target spells that as a temporary sequence, which allocates where the source did not.

display_method_reason: The source's `String() string` IS the target's `Display`. `fmt.Stringer` and `std::fmt::Display` are the same contract -- one method, no arguments, renders the receiver as text -- and every facility in each language that prints a value goes through its own one. So this is a mapping between the two standard libraries rather than a redesign of the type: emitting it as an inherent `fn string(&self) -> String` keeps the method and loses the contract, and the ported type then cannot be printed, formatted, or `to_string()`d by anything generic -- which is most of what a caller wants it for. Both review gates named `Version::string()` and `Address::string()` as evidence the code was translated rather than written.

channel_forms.reason:
THE SOURCE'S CHANNEL IS ONE VALUE CARRYING BOTH ENDS and the target's is a pair, so there is no single type here and there could not be: which end a site holds is a fact about where the channel is USED, and the transform settles that per parameter before asking for a spelling. A parameter the body only sends on is a sender; one it only receives from is a receiver; one it does both on has no single end and refuses.

TOKIO, because the operator asked for it by name and because the source's goroutine is a green thread -- a scheduler over stack-less tasks is the target's counterpart to a scheduler over stack-ful ones, where a thread per goroutine is not.

WHAT THIS KEEPS: a send that does not complete until a receiver takes the value, which the source's unbuffered channel promises and the target's bounded sender also promises; and a panic when the far end is gone, which is what the source does and what `expect` does.

WHAT IT DOES NOT KEEP, stated because it is the cost: `mpsc` is multi-producer and SINGLE-consumer where the source's channel is multi-consumer. A channel two sites receive from is not this, and the engine refuses it rather than emitting a fan-out the source never had. The source also chooses uniformly at random among ready `select` arms and this macro is biased unless told otherwise, which is why the select rule carries its own condition rather than riding on this table.
